title: Accuracy at sentence and word level

blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Write accurately: sentence boundaries, agreement, tense, punctuation and spelling; and the proofreading passes that catch each kind of error.

blocks.heading: The comma splice
blocks.text: A comma splice is two complete sentences joined by a comma alone — "the gates opened at six, the crowd was already waiting" — and it is the commonest sentence-boundary error. It is fixed three ways: a full stop makes two sentences, a semicolon joins two that belong together, or a conjunction with its comma does the joining the comma cannot. The splice is worth catching first in any proofread, because everything else is easier to see once the boundaries are honest.

blocks.heading: Fragments: error and choice
blocks.text: An accidental sentence fragment is an error; a deliberate minor sentence is a choice — and the difference is whether the grammar broke or the writer decided. "Not this time." is a choice: a minor sentence held for effect, and the writing around it shows the decision. "Because the gates opened." is an error: a subordinate clause with nothing to belong to, and the reader is left holding it. The proofread asks each fragment the same question — did I decide this? — and the answer decides whether it stays.

blocks.heading: Direct speech, punctuated and paragraphed
blocks.text: Direct speech is punctuated by its own rules: the marks around the words, the reporting clause and its comma, and a new paragraph for each new speaker. "There it is," she said, and pointed — the comma inside the marks, the reporting clause after, the action attached. When speech runs into the narrative without its punctuation or new paragraphs, the reader loses the map of the conversation: who said what becomes a crowd, and the paragraphing is the difference between a dialogue and a brawl.

blocks.heading: Drift: tense and capitals
blocks.text: Two errors of consistency are caught in the same proofread. Tense that drifts between past and present loses the reader’s sense of when the piece stands — "She opened the door and the hall is full of people" — and the fix is to choose one tense and check every verb against it. Missing capitals for sentence openings and proper nouns are the small, visible errors a final pass exists for: cheap to fix, costly in the impression they leave, and never worth the marks they lose.

blocks.heading: The proofreading passes
blocks.text: Proofreading is done as one read for each kind of error, because each pass has one thing to look for and finds it. First pass: sentence boundaries — splices and fragments. Second pass: agreement and tense — the verb against its subject, the tense against its neighbours. Third pass: capitals and proper nouns, speech punctuation, and the small rest. Three reads sound slow and are faster than one vague read, because the finding is what takes the time, and one thing at a time is findable.

blocks.heading: Worked example: three passes on one paragraph
blocks.text: A draft paragraph: "The market opens at six, by seven the stalls are full. she was selling oranges. the price was good and the oranges was sweet." First pass: "six, by seven" is a splice — full stop or semicolon; "she was selling oranges." is fine. Second pass: "the oranges was sweet" — agreement, "were". Third pass: "she" and "the price" need their capitals, and the tense — opened, was — wants one past throughout: "The market opened at six; by seven the stalls were full. She was selling oranges. The price was good and the oranges were sweet." Three passes, four fixes, one honest paragraph.
